Part 1

Neurons and perceptrons: the building blocks

Part 1 · Neurons

What is a neuron?

An artificial neuron is the basic unit of a neural network. A brain cell receives signals, combines them and sends a signal on; an artificial neuron does the same with simple arithmetic. (The simplest version, which uses a step activation, is called a perceptron.)

  • Inputs x1,x2,…,xnx_1, x_2, \dots, x_nx1​,x2​,…,xn​: the numbers fed into the neuron (e.g. the features)
  • Weights w1,w2,…,wnw_1, w_2, \dots, w_nw1​,w2​,…,wn​: how much each input matters
  • Bias bbb: an extra number that is added on; it shifts the point where the neuron “switches on”
  • Weighted sum zzz: multiply each input by its weight, add them up, add the bias
  • Activation function fff: a function applied to zzz, usually one that bends (non-linear)
  • Output yyy: the result, f(z)f(z)f(z)
z=w1x1+w2x2+⋯+wnxn+by=f(z)\begin{aligned} z &= w_1x_1 + w_2x_2 + \dots + w_nx_n + b \\ y &= f(z) \end{aligned}zy​=w1​x1​+w2​x2​+⋯+wn​xn​+b=f(z)​

New terms

Parameter
A number the model learns during training: here, the weights and biases. Training means adjusting them, a little at a time, until the outputs are close to the correct answers.
Sound familiar?
zzz is the same weighted sum as in linear and logistic regression: weights = coefficients, bias = intercept.

Part 1 · Neurons

Visual example

  • 3 inputs (x1,x2,x3x_1, x_2, x_3x1​,x2​,x3​) flow into a circle, the neuron’s “body”, which adds them up (Σ) with their weights and the bias, then applies the activation function. An output yyy flows out.
  • The arrows show the direction information flows.
  • Real neurons (right) work in a loosely similar way: dendrites collect incoming signals, the cell body combines them, and the axon sends a signal on.

Part 1 · Neurons

A simple example

Let’s calculate the output of one neuron by hand:

  • Inputs: x1=0.5x_1 = 0.5x1​=0.5, x2=0.3x_2 = 0.3x2​=0.3
  • Weights: w1=0.4w_1 = 0.4w1​=0.4, w2=0.7w_2 = 0.7w2​=0.7
  • Bias: b=0.1b = 0.1b=0.1
  • Activation: a step function: output 1 if z>0z > 0z>0, otherwise 0

Calculation:

z=(0.4×0.5)+(0.7×0.3)+0.1=0.2+0.21+0.1=0.51\begin{aligned} z &= (0.4 \times 0.5) + (0.7 \times 0.3) + 0.1 \\ &= 0.2 + 0.21 + 0.1 = 0.51 \end{aligned}z​=(0.4×0.5)+(0.7×0.3)+0.1=0.2+0.21+0.1=0.51​

Since z=0.51>0z = 0.51 > 0z=0.51>0, the output is y=1y = 1y=1.

Scaling up

Every neuron in a network does this same small calculation. Connect millions of them and the network can solve complex problems.

New term

Step function
An activation that jumps straight from 0 to 1 at a threshold, like an on/off switch.

Part 2

Activation functions: adding non-linearity

Part 2 · Activation functions

What are activation functions?

An activation function is applied to a neuron’s weighted sum. It decides whether the neuron “fires”, and how strongly: how much signal it passes on to the next layer.

Think of a dimmer switch: the weighted sum is how far you turn the knob, the activation function decides how bright the light gets.

New term

Non-linear
Any function whose graph is not a straight line (it bends, curves or has a corner).

Part 2 · Activation functions

Common activation functions

ReLU (Rectified Linear Unit)

f(z)=max⁡(0,z)f(z) = \max(0, z)f(z)=max(0,z)
  • In words: if zzz is negative, output 0; otherwise output zzz
  • Outputs: 0 or more, with no upper limit
  • Simple and fast to compute
  • Helps avoid the vanishing gradient problem (explained shortly)

Sigmoid

σ(z)=11+e−z\sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}σ(z)=1+e−z1​
  • Outputs: between 0 and 1 (never quite reaching either)
  • A smooth, S-shaped curve: the same function as in logistic regression
  • Problem: flat at both ends, which slows learning down (vanishing gradients, explained shortly)

New terms

max⁡(0,z)\max(0, z)max(0,z)
The larger of 0 and zzz.
eee
A mathematical constant, about 2.718 (as in Lecture 7A).
σ\sigmaσ
“sigma”, the usual symbol for the sigmoid function.

Part 2 · Activation functions

Why non-linearity is critical

  • Without non-linear activation functions, a neural network is just one big linear model, however many layers it has.
  • Stacking straight-line functions just gives another straight line. For example:
g(x)=3x+1,f(u)=2u+5    ⇒    f(g(x))=2(3x+1)+5=6x+7g(x) = 3x + 1,\quad f(u) = 2u + 5 \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; f(g(x)) = 2(3x + 1) + 5 = 6x + 7g(x)=3x+1,f(u)=2u+5⇒f(g(x))=2(3x+1)+5=6x+7
  • Two “layers”, but the result is still a straight line, 6x+76x + 76x+7.
  • Non-linearity lets networks learn curved decision boundaries and complex patterns that linear models can’t capture.

New term

f(g(x))f(g(x))f(g(x))
“f of g of x”: apply ggg first, then apply fff to the result. This is what stacking layers does.

Part 2 · Activation functions

Visualizing activation functions

Top: the two functions from the previous slide, for zzz from −5 to 5. Note ReLU’s sharp corner at zero.

Bottom: two more you may meet, just to show there are many other choices:

  • tanh: an S-curve centred at zero (between −1 and 1)
  • Leaky ReLU: a small slope for negative values, instead of a flat 0

Part 2 · Activation functions

The vanishing gradient problem

  • Networks learn by following gradients (slopes): how much the loss changes when a weight changes (Part 6).
  • The vanishing gradient problem: the slopes become tiny as they are passed back through the layers (backpropagation, Part 7), so the early layers barely learn.
  • This is a particular problem for sigmoid and tanh. Both curves are almost flat at each end, so when zzz is far from 0, their slope is close to 0.
    • Even at its steepest point, the sigmoid’s slope is only 0.25.
    • Backpropagation multiplies slopes layer by layer: over 10 layers, 0.2510≈0.0000010.25^{10} \approx 0.0000010.2510≈0.000001. The signal vanishes.
  • ReLU helps: its slope is exactly 1 for every positive input (and 0 for negative ones), so it doesn’t shrink the signal for positive values.

New terms

Gradient
The slope: how steeply the output rises or falls as you change an input.
Loss
A number measuring how wrong the network’s predictions are (Part 5).

Part 2 · Activation functions

Choosing the right activation function

WhereUsual choiceWhy
Hidden layersReLU or Leaky ReLUThe most common default
Output layer, binary classificationSigmoidGives one probability between 0 and 1
Output layer, multi-class classificationSoftmaxGives a probability for each class, adding up to 1
Output layer, regressionLinear (no activation), or ReLU if the output can’t be negativeThe output can be any number

New terms

Softmax
Turns a list of scores into probabilities that are all positive and add up to 1. The biggest score gets the biggest probability.
Multi-class
Classification with more than two classes (e.g. cat, dog or rabbit).
Regression
Predicting a number (e.g. a height) rather than a class.

Part 3

Network architecture: organizing neurons into layers

Part 3 · Architecture

What is a neural network architecture?

  • A network’s architecture is how its neurons are organized and connected.
  • The most basic architecture is the feedforward neural network: information flows one way, from input to output, with no loops.
  • A feedforward network built from fully connected layers is called a multilayer perceptron (MLP). That is what scikit-learn’s MLPClassifier and MLPRegressor build.

New terms

Layer
A column of neurons that all work at the same stage.
Feedforward
Signals only move forward, never back to an earlier layer.

Part 3 · Architecture

Layer types

Input layer

  • Receives the raw input data
  • Number of neurons = number of features in the data
  • No calculation happens here; it’s just the entry point

Hidden layers

  • Do the in-between calculations
  • There can be several (a deep network)
  • How many layers, and how many neurons in each, are hyperparameters you choose

Output layer

  • Produces the final prediction
  • Number of neurons depends on the task:
    • Regression: 1 neuron per number predicted (usually 1)
    • Binary classification: 1 neuron (with sigmoid)
    • Multi-class with kkk classes: kkk neurons (with softmax)

New terms

Hidden
Not directly seen: these layers sit between the input and the output.
Hyperparameter
A setting you choose before training (e.g. number of neurons), rather than one the network learns.
Deep learning
Using neural networks with many hidden layers.

Part 3 · Architecture

Fully connected (dense) layers

  • In a fully connected layer, every neuron in one layer is connected to every neuron in the next.
  • If a layer has nnn neurons and the next has mmm, there are n×mn \times mn×m weights connecting them, plus mmm biases (one per neuron in the next layer).

Example: the 3 → 4 → 2 network drawn two slides on

Input to hidden: 3×4=123 \times 4 = 123×4=12 weights + 4 biases = 16 parameters

Hidden to output: 4×2=84 \times 2 = 84×2=8 weights + 2 biases = 10 parameters

Total: 26 parameters for training to learn.

New term

Dense layer
Another name for a fully connected layer.

Part 3 · Architecture

Network depth and width

  • Depth: the number of layers (deep networks have many)
  • Width: the number of neurons in each layer

Deeper networks can learn more complex, step-by-step (hierarchical) features, but they are harder to train. Wider networks add capacity within each layer.

Example

In image recognition, early layers tend to pick up simple features such as edges, later layers combine them into shapes, and the last layers into whole objects.

New terms

Hierarchical
Built in levels, each level from the one below.
Capacity
How complex a pattern a model is able to represent.

Part 3 · Architecture

Visualizing network architecture

  • A feedforward neural network with an input layer (3 neurons), one hidden layer (4 neurons) and an output layer (2 neurons).
  • 2 outputs, e.g. predicting two numbers at once (one output neuron per number predicted).
  • Each circle is a neuron, stacked vertically within its layer; each line is one weight. The 20 weights and 6 biases are the 26 parameters counted two slides back.

Part 3 · Architecture

Architecture design considerations

Input layer size: set by your data, e.g. 784 for a 28 × 28 pixel image (one input per pixel).

Hidden layers:

  • Start simple (1–2 hidden layers)
  • Common sizes: 64, 128, 256 or 512 neurons
  • You can use decreasing sizes, e.g. [512, 256, 128]

Output layer size: set by your task (see “Layer types”).

In scikit-learn you only choose the hidden layers; the input and output sizes are worked out from your data.

Code

from sklearn.neural_network import MLPClassifier

# Two hidden layers: 128 neurons, then 64 neurons
model = MLPClassifier(hidden_layer_sizes=(128, 64),
                      max_iter=500, random_state=1)

Part 3 · Architecture

Universal approximation theorem

  • A neat theoretical result: a feedforward network with just one hidden layer, given enough neurons and a non-linear activation, can approximate any continuous function (over a limited range of inputs) as closely as you like.
  • It says such a network exists; it doesn’t say how many neurons you need, or that training will find it.
  • In practice, deeper networks often learn more efficiently and need fewer neurons in total.

New terms

Continuous function
A curve you can draw without lifting your pen.
Approximate
Get very close to, without necessarily being exact.

Part 4

Forward propagation: making predictions

Part 4 · Forward propagation

What is forward propagation?

Forward propagation is passing input data through the network to get a prediction. Data flows forward, layer by layer: each neuron calculates its output from the outputs of the layer before.

Like an assembly line: each station (layer) takes what the previous station produced, works on it, and passes it on.

In everyday use

Every time a trained model classifies an image, translates text or recommends a product, it is running one forward pass. Making the network learn comes next (Parts 5–7).

New term

Forward pass
One run of forward propagation, from inputs to prediction.

Part 4 · Forward propagation

The maths of a forward pass

For a network with LLL layers:

Layer 1:z[1]=W[1]x+b[1],a[1]=f[1](z[1])Layer l:z[l]=W[l]a[l−1]+b[l],a[l]=f[l](z[l])Output L:z[L]=W[L]a[L−1]+b[L],y^=f[L](z[L])\begin{aligned} \textbf{Layer 1:}\quad & z^{[1]} = W^{[1]}x + b^{[1]}, & a^{[1]} &= f^{[1]}(z^{[1]})\\ \textbf{Layer } l\textbf{:}\quad & z^{[l]} = W^{[l]}a^{[l-1]} + b^{[l]}, & a^{[l]} &= f^{[l]}(z^{[l]})\\ \textbf{Output } L\textbf{:}\quad & z^{[L]} = W^{[L]}a^{[L-1]} + b^{[L]}, & \hat{y} &= f^{[L]}(z^{[L]}) \end{aligned}Layer 1:Layer l:Output L:​z[1]=W[1]x+b[1],z[l]=W[l]a[l−1]+b[l],z[L]=W[L]a[L−1]+b[L],​a[1]a[l]y^​​=f[1](z[1])=f[l](z[l])=f[L](z[L])​

In words

Each layer takes weighted sums of the previous layer’s outputs, adds its biases, then applies its activation function. Repeat until you reach the output.

Reading the symbols

[l][l][l]
The layer number (a label, not a power).
W[l]W^{[l]}W[l]
The weights for layer lll, as a table (matrix) with one row per neuron.
b[l]b^{[l]}b[l]
The biases for layer lll, as a list (vector).
z[l]z^{[l]}z[l]
The weighted sums, before the activation.
a[l]a^{[l]}a[l]
The outputs after the activation (“activations”).
f[l]f^{[l]}f[l]
The activation function for layer lll.
xxx
The input features.
y^\hat{y}y^​
“y-hat”: the predicted output.

Part 4 · Forward propagation

Step-by-step example

  • A good animated visualization: https://mlu-explain.github.io/neural-networks/
  • A simple network: 2 inputs → 3 hidden neurons (ReLU) → 1 output (sigmoid)

Given:

  • Input: x=(0.5, 0.8)x = (0.5,\ 0.8)x=(0.5, 0.8)
  • Weights: W[1]=[0.20.50.30.40.10.6]W^{[1]} = \begin{bmatrix} 0.2 & 0.5 \\ 0.3 & 0.4 \\ 0.1 & 0.6 \end{bmatrix}W[1]=​0.20.30.1​0.50.40.6​​,   W[2]=[0.70.30.5]\;W^{[2]} = \begin{bmatrix} 0.7 & 0.3 & 0.5 \end{bmatrix}W[2]=[0.7​0.3​0.5​]
    Each row of W[1]W^{[1]}W[1] holds the 2 weights going into one hidden neuron.
  • Biases: b[1]=(0.1, 0.2, 0.1)b^{[1]} = (0.1,\ 0.2,\ 0.1)b[1]=(0.1, 0.2, 0.1),   b[2]=0.3\;b^{[2]} = 0.3b[2]=0.3

Layer 1 (one weighted sum per hidden neuron):

z1=0.2(0.5)+0.5(0.8)+0.1=0.60z2=0.3(0.5)+0.4(0.8)+0.2=0.67z3=0.1(0.5)+0.6(0.8)+0.1=0.63\begin{aligned} z_1 &= 0.2(0.5) + 0.5(0.8) + 0.1 = 0.60\\ z_2 &= 0.3(0.5) + 0.4(0.8) + 0.2 = 0.67\\ z_3 &= 0.1(0.5) + 0.6(0.8) + 0.1 = 0.63 \end{aligned}z1​z2​z3​​=0.2(0.5)+0.5(0.8)+0.1=0.60=0.3(0.5)+0.4(0.8)+0.2=0.67=0.1(0.5)+0.6(0.8)+0.1=0.63​

ReLU keeps positive numbers unchanged: a[1]=(0.60, 0.67, 0.63)a^{[1]} = (0.60,\ 0.67,\ 0.63)a[1]=(0.60, 0.67, 0.63)

Layer 2: z[2]=0.7(0.60)+0.3(0.67)+0.5(0.63)+0.3=1.236z^{[2]} = 0.7(0.60) + 0.3(0.67) + 0.5(0.63) + 0.3 = 1.236z[2]=0.7(0.60)+0.3(0.67)+0.5(0.63)+0.3=1.236

y^=σ(1.236)=11+e−1.236≈0.775\hat{y} = \sigma(1.236) = \dfrac{1}{1 + e^{-1.236}} \approx \mathbf{0.775}y^​=σ(1.236)=1+e−1.2361​≈0.775: a 77.5% probability of class 1.

Part 4 · Forward propagation · optional

Implementing forward propagation by hand (optional)

  • You don’t need to do this: it is for anyone curious about what happens “under the hood”.
  • In practice we use the ready-made MLPClassifier() or MLPRegressor() from sklearn.neural_network.
  • A simple two-layer forward pass: it takes the input X and each layer’s weights W and biases b, calculates the weighted sums (z), applies the activations (ReLU for the hidden layer, sigmoid for the output), and returns the prediction plus the in-between values that backpropagation needs.

Code

import numpy as np

# Simple forward propagation implementation
def forward_pass(X, W1, b1, W2, b2):
    # Hidden layer: compute z and apply ReLU
    z1 = np.dot(W1, X) + b1          # weighted sums for all hidden neurons at once
    a1 = np.maximum(0, z1)           # ReLU activation
    # Output layer: compute z and apply sigmoid
    z2 = np.dot(W2, a1) + b2
    y_pred = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z2))   # Sigmoid
    return y_pred, a1, z1            # Return intermediate values for backprop

Part 4 · Forward propagation · optional

Implementing forward propagation: running it (optional)

  • Run forward_pass() on the numbers from the step-by-step example. It gives the same answer we worked out by hand: 0.775.

Code

X  = np.array([0.5, 0.8])           # input
W1 = np.array([[0.2, 0.5],           # weights into hidden neuron 1
               [0.3, 0.4],           # ... hidden neuron 2
               [0.1, 0.6]])          # ... hidden neuron 3
b1 = np.array([0.1, 0.2, 0.1])
W2 = np.array([[0.7, 0.3, 0.5]])     # weights into the output neuron
b2 = np.array([0.3])

y_pred, a1, z1 = forward_pass(X, W1, b1, W2, b2)
print("z1 (hidden weighted sums):", z1.round(3))
print("a1 (after ReLU):          ", a1.round(3))
print("y_pred (probability):     ", y_pred.round(3))

Output

z1 (hidden weighted sums): [0.6  0.67 0.63]
a1 (after ReLU):           [0.6  0.67 0.63]
y_pred (probability):      [0.775]

Part 4 · Forward propagation

Vectorization: many examples at once

In practice we push a whole batch of examples through together using matrix arithmetic, instead of one at a time:

  • Input: XXX is a matrix where each column is one training example. (scikit-learn stores one example per row: same idea, turned sideways.)
  • Z[l]=W[l]A[l−1]+b[l]Z^{[l]} = W^{[l]}A^{[l-1]} + b^{[l]}Z[l]=W[l]A[l−1]+b[l]: the bias is added to every column (“broadcasting”)
  • Each column of Z[l]Z^{[l]}Z[l] and A[l]A^{[l]}A[l] belongs to one example

This vectorization makes the calculations dramatically faster, especially on GPUs.

New terms

Matrix
A table of numbers (capital letters such as XXX, WWW).
Vectorization
Doing a calculation on whole tables at once instead of looping one number at a time.
Batch
A group of examples processed together.
GPU
Graphics processing unit: a chip that does many simple calculations at the same time.

Part 5

Loss functions: measuring prediction quality

Part 5 · Loss functions

What is a loss function?

A loss function (or cost function) measures how wrong the network’s predictions are. It takes the predictions and the true labels and returns a single number: the “error” or “loss”.

Lower is better.

New term

True label
The correct answer for an example, written yyy (the prediction is y^\hat{y}y^​).

Part 5 · Loss functions

Loss vs. cost

  • Loss: the error for a single training example
  • Cost: the average loss over all training examples

For a dataset with mmm examples:

J=1m∑i=1mL(y^(i), y(i))J = \frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}L\big(\hat{y}^{(i)},\, y^{(i)}\big)J=m1​i=1∑m​L(y^​(i),y(i))

Reading the formula

∑i=1m\sum_{i=1}^{m}∑i=1m​
“Sum”: add up the loss for example 1, example 2, …, up to example mmm.
1m\frac{1}{m}m1​
Divide by the number of examples, which turns the total into an average.
(i)^{(i)}(i)
Example number iii (again a label, not a power).
JJJ
The usual letter for the cost.

Part 5 · Loss functions

Common loss functions

Mean squared error (MSE): regression

LMSE=(y^−y)2JMSE=1m∑i=1m(y^(i)−y(i))2L_{\text{MSE}} = (\hat{y} - y)^2 \qquad J_{\text{MSE}} = \frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\big(\hat{y}^{(i)} - y^{(i)}\big)^2LMSE​=(y^​−y)2JMSE​=m1​i=1∑m​(y^​(i)−y(i))2

When to use: regression problems, where you predict numbers.

  • Big errors count much more: an error of 2 adds 4, an error of 10 adds 100
  • A smooth curve with no corners, which suits gradient descent
  • Sensitive to outliers

Mean absolute error (MAE): regression

LMAE=∣y^−y∣JMAE=1m∑i=1m∣y^(i)−y(i)∣L_{\text{MAE}} = |\hat{y} - y| \qquad J_{\text{MAE}} = \frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\big|\hat{y}^{(i)} - y^{(i)}\big|LMAE​=∣y^​−y∣JMAE​=m1​i=1∑m​​y^​(i)−y(i)​

When to use: regression, when you want outliers to matter less.

  • Every unit of error counts the same
  • Less affected by outliers than MSE
  • Has a sharp corner at 0, where its slope isn’t defined

∣ ⋅ ∣|\,\cdot\,|∣⋅∣ means the size of a number, ignoring its sign: ∣−3∣=3|-3| = 3∣−3∣=3.

Binary cross-entropy: binary classification

LBCE=−[ ylog⁡(y^)+(1−y)log⁡(1−y^) ]L_{\text{BCE}} = -\big[\,y\log(\hat{y}) + (1-y)\log(1-\hat{y})\,\big]LBCE​=−[ylog(y^​)+(1−y)log(1−y^​)]

When to use: classification with two classes, with a sigmoid output (y^\hat{y}y^​ is a probability). It is the same loss logistic regression uses.

  • Punishes confident wrong answers heavily. If the true class is 1: predicting 0.9 gives a loss of 0.11; predicting 0.1 gives 2.30.
  • Works naturally with probability outputs

Only one term is “on” for each example: if y=1y = 1y=1 the loss is −log⁡(y^)-\log(\hat{y})−log(y^​); if y=0y = 0y=0 it is −log⁡(1−y^)-\log(1-\hat{y})−log(1−y^​). Here log⁡\loglog is the natural log.

Categorical cross-entropy: multi-class classification

LCCE=−∑j=1kyjlog⁡(y^j)L_{\text{CCE}} = -\sum_{j=1}^{k} y_j\log(\hat{y}_j)LCCE​=−j=1∑k​yj​log(y^​j​)

yyy is one-hot encoded and y^j\hat{y}_jy^​j​ is the predicted probability of class jjj (from softmax).

When to use: classification with more than two classes.

  • Used with a softmax output layer; each class gets its own output neuron
  • Because yyy is all 0s except one 1, the loss is simply −log⁡(probability given to the correct class)-\log(\text{probability given to the correct class})−log(probability given to the correct class)
  • Minimizing it is the same idea as maximum likelihood (Lecture 7A)

New term

One-hot encoding
Writing a class as a list with a 1 for the true class and 0s elsewhere. With classes (cat, dog, rabbit), “dog” is (0, 1, 0).

Part 5 · Loss functions

Visualizing loss functions

  • MSE and MAE plotted against the prediction error.
  • MSE’s curve (a parabola) shows how it punishes large errors much more severely than MAE’s straight-line V.
  • That is why MSE is more sensitive to outliers: one big error can dominate the total.

Part 5 · Loss functions

How loss functions guide learning

The loss function defines what training tries to minimize. Picture it as a landscape: each position is one choice of weights, and the height is the loss. Different loss functions create different landscapes:

  • Convex (bowl-shaped) losses, like MSE for linear regression, have a single lowest point.
  • Non-convex losses, like those of deep neural networks, have many valleys (local minima).
  • The choice of loss affects both what the model learns and how easily it can be trained.
  • When we say we “train” or “fit” a model, or that a model “learns”, we mean: minimize the loss function.
  • If the loss can’t be made small enough, the model “fails to learn”: we can’t train it well on the dataset.
What is “enough”?

There’s no universal number. Compare the loss with a simple baseline (e.g. always predicting the most common class, or the average value) and with what your application needs. Judge it on validation data, not just the training data.

New terms

Minimum
A lowest point. The global minimum is the lowest point of all; a local minimum is only lower than its surroundings.
Convex
Shaped like a bowl, with one bottom.

Part 5 · Loss functions

Practical considerations

Classification: why not MSE?

  • Use cross-entropy (binary or categorical) with a sigmoid or softmax output
  • With MSE, the slopes become tiny when the model is confidently wrong, so learning stalls exactly when it most needs to move

Custom problems

  • You can design your own loss function that builds in knowledge of your field
  • It should be differentiable (a few sharp corners, like MAE’s, are OK)
  • Why?
Why must the loss be differentiable?

Training uses gradient descent (next part), which needs the slope of the loss to know which direction to change each weight. No slope, no direction.

New term

Differentiable
Has a well-defined slope at every point (a smooth curve, without gaps or jumps).

Part 6

Gradient descent: how the network learns

The engine that powers neural-network training

Part 6 · Gradient descent

What is gradient descent?

Gradient descent is a step-by-step method for finding the lowest point of a function. In neural networks, we use it to find the weights and biases that make the loss as small as possible.

It is the same idea that fitted the coefficients in logistic regression (Lecture 7A, “Where did the w’s come from?”).

New terms

Optimization
Searching for the best values of some numbers (here: the values that minimize the loss).
Iterative
Done in repeated rounds, each one improving a little on the last.

Part 6 · Gradient descent

The intuition

Imagine standing on a hillside in thick fog (the loss landscape) and wanting to reach the lowest valley. Gradient descent is:

  1. Feel which way the ground slopes most steeply downhill
  2. Take a step in that direction
  3. Repeat until you reach a valley floor (a minimum)

Translating the picture

Your position = the current weights and biases. The height = the loss. The slope = the gradient. The step size = the learning rate.

Part 6 · Gradient descent

The gradient

The gradient ∇J\nabla J∇J is the list of slopes of the loss, one for each weight. It points in the direction where the loss rises most steeply:

∇J=[∂J∂w1∂J∂w2⋮∂J∂wn]\nabla J = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{\partial J}{\partial w_1} \\[6pt] \dfrac{\partial J}{\partial w_2} \\ \vdots \\ \dfrac{\partial J}{\partial w_n} \end{bmatrix}∇J=​∂w1​∂J​∂w2​∂J​⋮∂wn​∂J​​​

To make the loss smaller, we step in the opposite direction (downhill). How big a step is set by the learning rate α\alphaα (alpha), a hyperparameter. The next slide gives the exact rule.

Reading the symbols

∂J∂w1\dfrac{\partial J}{\partial w_1}∂w1​∂J​
“Partial derivative”: the slope of JJJ when only w1w_1w1​ changes and everything else is held fixed. Roughly: if I nudge w1w_1w1​ up a little, how much does the loss change?
∇\nabla∇ (nabla)
“Gradient of”: collect all those slopes into one list.
⋮\vdots⋮
“And so on” down the list.

Part 6 · Gradient descent

The update rule

For each parameter (any weight or bias), the update is:

θnew=θold−α ∂J∂θ\theta_{\text{new}} = \theta_{\text{old}} - \alpha\,\frac{\partial J}{\partial \theta}θnew​=θold​−α∂θ∂J​

In words: new value = old value − (step size × slope).

  • θ\thetaθ (theta) stands for any one parameter (a weight or a bias)
  • α\alphaα is the learning rate (typically 0.001 to 0.1)
  • ∂J∂θ\dfrac{\partial J}{\partial \theta}∂θ∂J​ is the slope of the loss with respect to that parameter

Why the minus sign?

If the slope is positive, increasing θ\thetaθ increases the loss, so we should decrease θ\thetaθ. If the slope is negative, we increase it. Subtracting the slope does both automatically.

Part 6 · Gradient descent

Variants of gradient descent

They differ in how many training examples are used to work out each step:

1. Batch gradient descent

  • Uses the entire training set for each step
  • Pros: exact gradient, steady progress
  • Cons: slow on large datasets; can settle in a local minimum

2. Stochastic gradient descent (SGD)

  • Uses one example at a time
  • Pros: fast updates; the randomness can shake it out of local minima
  • Cons: noisy, zig-zagging steps; never settles exactly

3. Mini-batch gradient descent

  • Uses a small batch (e.g. 32, 64 or 128 examples)
  • Best of both: reasonably fast and reasonably steady
  • The most common choice in practice (often still just called “SGD”)

New terms

Stochastic
Involving randomness: the examples are picked in a random order.
Epoch
One full pass through the whole training set. Training usually runs for many epochs.
Converge
Settle down to a stable answer.

Part 6 · Gradient descent

The learning rate

The learning rate α\alphaα (the step size) is crucial:

  • Too large: the steps overshoot the valley; the loss bounces around or even grows (diverges)
  • Too small: tiny steps, so training takes very long
  • Just right: reaches a good minimum efficiently

Common strategies:

  • Start with 0.001 or 0.01
  • Use a learning-rate schedule: big steps early, smaller steps later
  • Use an adaptive method such as Adam or RMSprop, which adjusts the step size for each parameter automatically (Adam is scikit-learn’s default for MLPClassifier)

New terms

Diverge
Get further from the answer instead of closer; the loss keeps growing.
Adam, RMSprop
Popular improved versions of gradient descent. You can use them without knowing their details.

Part 6 · Gradient descent

Visualizing gradient descent

  • Gradient descent on the simplest “loss”: f(x)=x2f(x) = x^2f(x)=x2, whose slope is 2x2x2x.
  • Starting from x=4x = 4x=4 with learning rate 0.1, each step is x←x−0.1×2xx \leftarrow x - 0.1 \times 2xx←x−0.1×2x: 4 → 3.2 → 2.56 → 2.05 → …
  • The red dots show each step moving towards the minimum at x=0x = 0x=0.
  • The steps get smaller as it gets closer, because the slope gets flatter near the bottom.

Part 6 · Gradient descent

Challenges with gradient descent

  • Local minima: the algorithm can settle in a valley that isn’t the lowest one
  • Saddle points: places where the slope is zero but it isn’t a minimum (downhill in one direction, uphill in another, like a horse’s saddle)
  • Plateaus: flat regions where the slopes are tiny, so progress is very slow
  • Ill-conditioning: the landscape is much steeper in some directions than others, like a long narrow canyon, so steps zig-zag between the walls

These challenges are why improved optimizers such as Adam exist. We won’t go into their details in this course.

Part 7

Backpropagation: computing gradients efficiently

Part 7 · Backpropagation

What is backpropagation?

Gradient descent needs the slope of the loss with respect to every weight and bias. Backpropagation (short for “backward propagation of errors”) is the algorithm that calculates all of those slopes. It is the most important algorithm in deep learning, because it makes training deep networks feasible.

A network with millions of parameters needs millions of slopes, and working each one out separately would take far too long. Backpropagation gets round this by:

  • using the chain rule from calculus (next slide)
  • reusing calculations that are shared between many slopes
  • getting all the slopes in a single backward pass

Forward and backward

The forward pass sends the inputs forward to get a prediction and a loss. The backward pass sends the error backward, layer by layer, to find out how much each weight contributed to it.

New term

Chain rule
The calculus rule for the slope of a chain of functions, where one feeds into the next.

Part 7 · Backpropagation

The chain rule: the foundation

The chain rule breaks a complicated slope into simpler pieces. If xxx affects yyy, and yyy affects zzz:

dzdx=dzdy⋅dydx\frac{dz}{dx} = \frac{dz}{dy} \cdot \frac{dy}{dx}dxdz​=dydz​⋅dxdy​
  • In words: multiply together the effects of each step. (How xxx affects zzz) = (how xxx affects yyy) × (how yyy affects zzz).
  • Everyday version: if 1 hour of study raises your score by 2 points, and each point is worth $5 of prize money, then 1 hour of study is worth 2 × 5 = $10.

In a network, a weight in layer lll affects the loss through every later layer, so the chain has many links:

∂J∂w[l]=∂J∂a[L]⋅∂a[L]∂z[L]⋯∂a[l]∂z[l]⋅∂z[l]∂w[l]\frac{\partial J}{\partial w^{[l]}} = \frac{\partial J}{\partial a^{[L]}} \cdot \frac{\partial a^{[L]}}{\partial z^{[L]}} \cdots \frac{\partial a^{[l]}}{\partial z^{[l]}} \cdot \frac{\partial z^{[l]}}{\partial w^{[l]}}∂w[l]∂J​=∂a[L]∂J​⋅∂z[L]∂a[L]​⋯∂z[l]∂a[l]​⋅∂w[l]∂z[l]​

Read it right to left: how the weight changes zzz in its own layer, how that changes the activation, how that feeds the next layer, … all the way to the loss.

New term

dzdx\dfrac{dz}{dx}dxdz​
“The derivative of zzz with respect to xxx”: how fast zzz changes when xxx changes. The same thing as a slope.

Part 7 · Backpropagation · optional

The backpropagation algorithm (optional)

For a network with LLL layers. The key quantity is δ[l]\delta^{[l]}δ[l] (delta): how much the loss would change if layer lll’s weighted sums z[l]z^{[l]}z[l] changed, i.e. the “error signal” at layer lll. Good visualization: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ilg3gGewQ5U

Step 1: forward pass

Compute all weighted sums z[l]z^{[l]}z[l] and activations a[l]a^{[l]}a[l] for every layer, and the loss.

Step 2: error at the output layer

δ[L]=∂J∂a[L]⊙f′[L](z[L])\delta^{[L]} = \frac{\partial J}{\partial a^{[L]}} \odot f'^{[L]}(z^{[L]})δ[L]=∂a[L]∂J​⊙f′[L](z[L])

Reading the symbols

⊙\odot⊙
Multiply element by element (first with first, second with second, …).
f′f'f′
The derivative (slope) of the activation function.
WTW^TWT
The transpose: the weight table flipped so rows become columns. It sends the error backwards along the same connections.

Step 3: backward pass

For l=L−1,L−2,…,1l = L-1, L-2, \dots, 1l=L−1,L−2,…,1, pass the error back through the weights:

δ[l]=(W[l+1])Tδ[l+1]⊙f′[l](z[l])\delta^{[l]} = \big(W^{[l+1]}\big)^T \delta^{[l+1]} \odot f'^{[l]}(z^{[l]})δ[l]=(W[l+1])Tδ[l+1]⊙f′[l](z[l])

Step 4: slopes for the parameters

∂J∂W[l]=δ[l](a[l−1])T∂J∂b[l]=δ[l]\frac{\partial J}{\partial W^{[l]}} = \delta^{[l]}\big(a^{[l-1]}\big)^T \qquad \frac{\partial J}{\partial b^{[l]}} = \delta^{[l]}∂W[l]∂J​=δ[l](a[l−1])T∂b[l]∂J​=δ[l]

Then gradient descent (Part 6) uses these slopes to update every weight and bias.

Part 7 · Backpropagation · optional

Putting everything together: an example (optional)

A small network: input (2) → hidden (2, ReLU) → output (1, linear, i.e. no activation). Loss for one example: J=12(y^−y)2J = \tfrac{1}{2}(\hat{y} - y)^2J=21​(y^​−y)2 (squared error; the ½ just makes the slope tidier).

Forward pass

  1. z[1]=W[1]x+b[1]z^{[1]} = W^{[1]}x + b^{[1]}z[1]=W[1]x+b[1]
  2. a[1]=ReLU(z[1])a^{[1]} = \text{ReLU}(z^{[1]})a[1]=ReLU(z[1])
  3. z[2]=W[2]a[1]+b[2]z^{[2]} = W^{[2]}a^{[1]} + b^{[2]}z[2]=W[2]a[1]+b[2]
  4. y^=z[2]\hat{y} = z^{[2]}y^​=z[2] (linear output)
  5. J=12(y^−y)2J = \tfrac{1}{2}(\hat{y} - y)^2J=21​(y^​−y)2

Backward pass

Output error: ∂J∂y^=y^−y\dfrac{\partial J}{\partial \hat{y}} = \hat{y} - y∂y^​∂J​=y^​−y, and since the output is linear, δ[2]=y^−y\delta^{[2]} = \hat{y} - yδ[2]=y^​−y. The error signal is just “prediction minus truth”.

Hidden error: δ[1]=(W[2])Tδ[2]⊙ReLU′(z[1])\delta^{[1]} = \big(W^{[2]}\big)^T \delta^{[2]} \odot \text{ReLU}'(z^{[1]})δ[1]=(W[2])Tδ[2]⊙ReLU′(z[1]), where ReLU′(z)=1\text{ReLU}'(z) = 1ReLU′(z)=1 if z>0z > 0z>0, else 000. A hidden neuron that was switched off (z≤0z \le 0z≤0) gets no error signal.

Slopes: ∂J∂W[2]=δ[2](a[1])T\dfrac{\partial J}{\partial W^{[2]}} = \delta^{[2]}\big(a^{[1]}\big)^T∂W[2]∂J​=δ[2](a[1])T,   ∂J∂b[2]=δ[2]\;\dfrac{\partial J}{\partial b^{[2]}} = \delta^{[2]}∂b[2]∂J​=δ[2],   ∂J∂W[1]=δ[1]xT\;\dfrac{\partial J}{\partial W^{[1]}} = \delta^{[1]}x^T∂W[1]∂J​=δ[1]xT,   ∂J∂b[1]=δ[1]\;\dfrac{\partial J}{\partial b^{[1]}} = \delta^{[1]}∂b[1]∂J​=δ[1]

Part 7 · Backpropagation

Computational efficiency

Backpropagation matters because it is efficient, which is what makes it practical. Let WWW be the total number of weights:

  • Forward pass: about WWW operations (each weight is used once)
  • Backward pass: also about WWW operations
  • Total: still proportional to WWW

Without backpropagation, you would estimate each slope by nudging one weight and re-running the whole forward pass: WWW forward passes of WWW operations each, about W2W^2W2 in total. For a network with a million weights, that is a million times slower.

New term

O(W)O(W)O(W)
“Order WWW”: the amount of work grows in proportion to WWW. O(W2)O(W^2)O(W2) grows with the square of WWW.

Part 7 · Backpropagation

Common derivatives in backpropagation

The slopes that backpropagation plugs into the chain rule:

Activation functions

Sigmoid:σ′(z)=σ(z)(1−σ(z))ReLU:ReLU′(z)={1if z>00otherwise\begin{aligned} \text{Sigmoid:}\quad & \sigma'(z) = \sigma(z)\big(1 - \sigma(z)\big)\\[4pt] \text{ReLU:}\quad & \text{ReLU}'(z) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } z > 0 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \end{aligned}Sigmoid:ReLU:​σ′(z)=σ(z)(1−σ(z))ReLU′(z)={10​if z>0otherwise​​

The sigmoid’s slope is at most 0.25 (at z=0z = 0z=0): the root of the vanishing-gradient problem from Part 2.

Loss functions

Squared error:∂∂y^ 12(y^−y)2=y^−yBinary cross-entropy:∂∂y^[−ylog⁡y^−(1−y)log⁡(1−y^)]=y^−yy^(1−y^)\begin{aligned} \text{Squared error:}\quad & \frac{\partial}{\partial \hat{y}}\,\tfrac{1}{2}(\hat{y}-y)^2 = \hat{y} - y\\[4pt] \text{Binary cross-entropy:}\quad & \frac{\partial}{\partial \hat{y}}\big[-y\log\hat{y}-(1-y)\log(1-\hat{y})\big] = \frac{\hat{y}-y}{\hat{y}(1-\hat{y})} \end{aligned}Squared error:Binary cross-entropy:​∂y^​∂​21​(y^​−y)2=y^​−y∂y^​∂​[−ylogy^​−(1−y)log(1−y^​)]=y^​(1−y^​)y^​−y​​

A neat result: with a sigmoid output and cross-entropy loss, the two slopes multiply to give simply y^−y\hat{y} - yy^​−y.

Part 7 · Backpropagation

Why backpropagation is revolutionary

Before backpropagation was popularized in the 1980s, training multi-layer networks was considered impractical. Backpropagation made it possible to:

  • train deep networks efficiently
  • scale to millions (now billions) of parameters
  • learn complex, layered representations
  • power modern deep learning applications

Its weak spot

Because slopes are multiplied layer by layer, they can shrink to nothing (vanishing gradients, Part 2) or grow out of control (exploding gradients: the weights blow up). Much of modern network design (ReLU, batch normalization, careful starting weights) exists to keep the gradients healthy.

Part 8

Overfitting and regularization: making sure it generalizes

Part 8 · Overfitting

What is overfitting?

Overfitting happens when a model learns the training data too well, including its noise and quirks, and then fails on new, unseen data. The model has memorized the training set instead of learning the underlying pattern.

Signs of overfitting:

  • Training performance keeps improving while validation performance flattens or gets worse
  • So a large, growing gap opens up between the two

New terms

Training set
The data the model learns from.
Validation set
Data held back from training, used during development to check progress and choose settings.
Test set
Data kept untouched until the very end, for a final honest score.
Generalize
Work well on new data, not just the data the model was trained on.

Part 8 · Overfitting

Revisiting the bias–variance tradeoff

Bias

Error from a model that is too simple for the pattern, so it is wrong in a consistent way.

  • High bias → underfitting
  • Low bias → the model can capture complex patterns

Variance

Error from being too sensitive to the particular training data you happened to get.

  • High variance → overfitting (the model is too complex for the amount of data)
  • Low variance → stable predictions

The tradeoff: for a regression model’s expected test error,

Total error=Bias2+Variance+Irreducible error\text{Total error} = \text{Bias}^2 + \text{Variance} + \text{Irreducible error}Total error=Bias2+Variance+Irreducible error

Making a model more complex lowers bias but raises variance. Our goal is the sweet spot where the total is smallest.

New term

Irreducible error
Noise in the data that no model could ever predict.

Part 8 · Overfitting

Visualizing overfitting

  • A noisy sine-wave dataset (blue dots) and the true pattern (green dashes).
  • 3 models: an underfit model (too simple: a straight line), a good fit, and an overfit model (too complex: it chases every noisy point, and swings wildly between them).

Part 8 · Regularization

Regularization techniques

Regularization is any technique that discourages a model from overfitting. Six common ones:

L2 regularization (weight decay)

Add a penalty to the loss that discourages large weights:

Jregularized=J+λ2m∑all weightsw2J_{\text{regularized}} = J + \frac{\lambda}{2m}\sum_{\text{all weights}} w^2Jregularized​=J+2mλ​all weights∑​w2
  • λ\lambdaλ (lambda) sets how strong the penalty is (a hyperparameter)
  • The sum is over every weight in every layer; biases are usually not penalized
  • Effect on each gradient-descent step: the weight is first shrunk by a factor (1−αλm)\big(1 - \alpha\tfrac{\lambda}{m}\big)(1−αmλ​), then updated as usual. Hence the name weight decay: weights shrink slightly every step.

Why it works:

  • Smaller weights → a smoother, simpler model → less overfitting
  • Stops any single feature from having too much influence
  • In scikit-learn: the alpha setting of MLPClassifier

L1 regularization

Penalizes the absolute values of the weights instead of their squares:

Jregularized=J+λm∑all weights∣w∣J_{\text{regularized}} = J + \frac{\lambda}{m}\sum_{\text{all weights}} |w|Jregularized​=J+mλ​all weights∑​∣w∣

Key difference from L2:

  • Tends to push many weights to exactly zero (“sparse” weights)
  • So it effectively selects features: inputs with zero weight are ignored
  • Less commonly used in deep learning than L2

Dropout

During training, randomly switch off (set to zero) a fraction of the neurons:

Training:

  • For each training example and each layer, keep each neuron with probability ppp (e.g. 0.5 or 0.8)
  • Scale the surviving outputs up by 1/p1/p1/p, so the total signal stays about the same

Testing: use all neurons, with no dropout. The scaling during training means the outputs match on average.

Typical keep rates: 0.5 for hidden layers; 0.8, or no dropout, for the input layer

Why it works:

  • Neurons can’t rely on specific other neurons being there, so each has to learn something useful on its own
  • Every training step uses a different “thinned” network
  • Like training a huge ensemble of networks and averaging them
  • Very effective in practice, especially for fully connected layers

Early stopping

Watch the validation loss during training and stop when it stops improving:

Algorithm:

  1. Train the model
  2. After each epoch, measure the loss on the validation set
  3. If it hasn’t improved for nnn epochs (the patience), stop
  4. Keep the weights from the best validation epoch

Typical patience: 5–20 epochs

Why it works:

  • Stops the model training long enough to memorize the training data
  • Simple and effective
  • No extra computing cost
  • In scikit-learn: MLPClassifier(early_stopping=True)

Data augmentation

Make the training set bigger by creating altered copies of the examples you have:

For images:

  • Random rotations, flips, crops
  • Small changes to colour and brightness
  • Mixup: blend two images together

For text:

  • Replace words with synonyms
  • Back-translation: translate to another language and back

Why it works:

  • More training data → better generalization
  • The model learns what doesn’t matter (a cat is still a cat when rotated)
  • Bigger effective dataset without collecting new data

Batch normalization

Inside the network, rescale each layer’s weighted sums so that, within each mini-batch, they have mean 0 and spread 1:

z^=z−μbatchσbatch2+ϵz~=γz^+β\hat{z} = \frac{z - \mu_{\text{batch}}}{\sqrt{\sigma^2_{\text{batch}} + \epsilon}} \qquad \tilde{z} = \gamma\hat{z} + \betaz^=σbatch2​+ϵ​z−μbatch​​z~=γz^+β
  • μbatch\mu_{\text{batch}}μbatch​ and σbatch2\sigma^2_{\text{batch}}σbatch2​: the mean and variance of zzz over the batch; ϵ\epsilonϵ is a tiny number that avoids dividing by zero
  • γ\gammaγ and β\betaβ are learned, so the network can undo the rescaling if that helps

Benefits:

  • Allows higher learning rates, so training is faster
  • Less sensitive to the initial random weights
  • Acts as a mild regularizer, because each example is normalized with a different random batch
  • Mainly a training aid; the regularizing effect is a bonus

Part 8 · Regularization

Combining regularization techniques

In practice, several techniques are often used together.

A typical recipe:

  • L2 regularization with λ\lambdaλ between 0.001 and 0.01
  • Dropout with keep rate p=0.5p = 0.5p=0.5 in the hidden layers
  • Early stopping with patience = 10
  • Data augmentation, if it suits the data
  • Batch normalization in deep networks

Part 8 · Regularization

Monitoring for overfitting

  • A typical training run: plot the training loss and validation loss after every epoch.
  • At first both fall together: the model is learning.
  • After a certain point the training loss keeps falling while the validation loss starts to rise: the classic signature of overfitting.
  • That is the moment to apply regularization, or where early stopping would stop.

Part 8 · Regularization

Choosing the regularization strength

Grid search

  1. Try λ∈{0.0001,0.001,0.01,0.1}\lambda \in \{0.0001, 0.001, 0.01, 0.1\}λ∈{0.0001,0.001,0.01,0.1}
  2. Measure validation performance for each
  3. Keep the value that does best

Signs you need more

  • The signs of overfitting from the start of this part: validation falls behind training
  • Some weights have become very large

Signs you have too much

  • Both training and validation performance are poor
  • The model underfits (high bias)
  • Learning is very slow

New terms

Grid search
Trying every value in a list of candidate settings and keeping the best.
λ∈{… }\lambda \in \{\dots\}λ∈{…}
“λ\lambdaλ is one of” the values in the curly brackets.

Part 9

Evaluation metrics: measuring model performance

Part 9 · Evaluation

Why accuracy isn’t enough

Accuracy (the percentage of correct predictions) is intuitive, but it can mislead, especially with:

  • Imbalanced data: if 95% of emails are not spam, a “model” that says “not spam” to everything scores 95% accuracy while catching no spam at all
  • Unequal costs of errors: missing a cancer is far worse than a false alarm
  • Several classes: which classes are getting mixed up?

We need more informative metrics. The metric you choose defines what “better” means: pick the wrong one and you optimize for the wrong goal.

New terms

Metric
A number that scores how well a model performs.
Imbalanced
One class is much more common than the other(s).

Part 9 · Evaluation

Classification metrics

Confusion matrix

The foundation for most classification metrics (seen in Lecture 7A): a table of what the model predicted against what was true.

Predicted positivePredicted negative
Actually positiveTrue positive (TP)False negative (FN)
Actually negativeFalse positive (FP)True negative (TN)

Example: disease diagnosis (“positive” = has the disease)

  • TP: sick patients correctly identified
  • TN: healthy patients correctly identified
  • FP: healthy patients diagnosed as sick (a false alarm, “type I error”)
  • FN: sick patients diagnosed as healthy (a miss, “type II error”)

Precision

Definition: of everything the model called positive, what fraction really was positive?

Precision=TPTP+FP\text{Precision} = \frac{TP}{TP + FP}Precision=TP+FPTP​

Prioritize it when false positives are costly:

  • Spam filters: users hate real emails landing in spam
  • Product recommendations
  • Drug discovery: each candidate is expensive to test

Example

A spam filter flags 100 emails as spam, but only 80 of them really are spam:

Precision=80100=0.80\text{Precision} = \dfrac{80}{100} = 0.80Precision=10080​=0.80

Recall (also called sensitivity)

Definition: of everything that really was positive, what fraction did the model find?

Recall=TPTP+FN\text{Recall} = \frac{TP}{TP + FN}Recall=TP+FNTP​

Prioritize it when false negatives are costly:

  • Disease diagnosis: missing a disease is dangerous
  • Fraud detection: missed fraud costs money
  • Security systems

Example (same filter)

There were 120 spam emails in total and the filter caught 80 of them:

Recall=80120≈0.67\text{Recall} = \dfrac{80}{120} \approx 0.67Recall=12080​≈0.67

F1-score

Definition: a single number that balances precision and recall (their harmonic mean):

F1=2⋅Precision×RecallPrecision+Recall=2 TP2 TP+FP+FNF_1 = 2 \cdot \frac{\text{Precision} \times \text{Recall}}{\text{Precision} + \text{Recall}} = \frac{2\,TP}{2\,TP + FP + FN}F1​=2⋅Precision+RecallPrecision×Recall​=2TP+FP+FN2TP​

Why a harmonic mean? It is dragged down by whichever of the two is lower. Precision 1.0 with recall 0.1 gives F1≈0.18F_1 \approx 0.18F1​≈0.18, not 0.55. You can’t score well by being good at just one.

When to use: when you want one metric that rewards both precision and recall, e.g. with imbalanced classes.

Example (same filter)

Precision = 0.80, Recall = 0.67:

F1=2⋅0.80×0.670.80+0.67≈0.73F_1 = 2 \cdot \dfrac{0.80 \times 0.67}{0.80 + 0.67} \approx 0.73F1​=2⋅0.80+0.670.80×0.67​≈0.73

ROC curve and AUC

ROC (Receiver Operating Characteristic) curve:

  • A classifier gives a probability; you choose a threshold (e.g. 0.5) above which it says “positive”
  • The ROC curve plots the true positive rate (recall) against the false positive rate, for every possible threshold
  • FPR=FPFP+TN\text{FPR} = \dfrac{FP}{FP + TN}FPR=FP+TNFP​: the share of real negatives wrongly flagged

AUC (Area Under the Curve):

  • One number summarizing the whole ROC curve, from 0 to 1
  • Random guessing: AUC = 0.5. Perfect: AUC = 1.0
  • Meaning: AUC = 0.9 means that if you pick one random positive and one random negative example, there is a 90% chance the model gives the positive one the higher score

Multi-class classification (optional)

Precision and recall are defined for one class at a time. With kkk classes, you can calculate them for each class and then average:

Macro-average: calculate the metric for each class, then take the plain average:

Macro-precision=1k∑i=1kPrecisioni\text{Macro-precision} = \frac{1}{k}\sum_{i=1}^{k}\text{Precision}_iMacro-precision=k1​i=1∑k​Precisioni​

Treats all classes equally, regardless of their size.

Micro-average: pool the counts from all classes first:

Micro-precision=∑i=1kTPi∑i=1k(TPi+FPi)\text{Micro-precision} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{k}TP_i}{\sum_{i=1}^{k}(TP_i + FP_i)}Micro-precision=∑i=1k​(TPi​+FPi​)∑i=1k​TPi​​

Weighted by class size, so large classes count more.

Part 9 · Evaluation

Confusion matrix visualization

  • A confusion matrix for a 3-class problem (150 test images of cats, dogs and rabbits).
  • The diagonal (dark blue) shows correct predictions; everything off the diagonal is a mistake.
  • Each number says how many examples of a true class were predicted as each class, so you can see exactly which classes get confused: here, 8 dogs were called rabbits.
  • Accuracy = (45 + 38 + 43) / 150 = 84%, but the matrix tells you where the 16% went.

Part 9 · Evaluation

Choosing the right metric

For classification
Balanced classes, equal error costsAccuracy
Imbalanced classesF1-score, AUC
False positives costlyPrecision
False negatives costlyRecall
Comparing thresholdsROC curve, AUC
Probabilities must be trustworthyLog loss (cross-entropy)
For regression
General purposeRMSE (root mean squared error): punishes large errors, in the units of yyy
Outliers presentMAE: more robust
Want “% off” interpretationMAPE (mean absolute percentage error)
Comparing modelsR2R^2R2: unit-free, the share of variation explained (Lecture 4A)

New terms

RMSE
The square root of the MSE, which brings it back to the same units as the thing being predicted.
Log loss
The cross-entropy loss used as a metric: it rewards well-calibrated probabilities, not just correct labels.

Part 9 · Evaluation

Cross-validation

A single train/test split gives one noisy estimate of a metric. To get a reliable one:

k-fold cross-validation:

  1. Split the data into kkk equal parts, called folds (typically k=5k = 5k=5 or 101010)
  2. Train on k−1k-1k−1 folds, test on the remaining fold
  3. Repeat kkk times, so each fold is the test set once
  4. Average the metric over all kkk rounds

Benefits:

  • A more reliable estimate: less luck of the draw from one particular split
  • Every example is used for both training and testing

5-fold cross-validation:

Round 1
Round 2
Round 3
Round 4
Round 5

train test

Code

from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score

# 5 rounds; returns one accuracy score per round
scores = cross_val_score(model, X, y, cv=5)
print(scores.mean())

Wrap-up

Conclusion: how it all fits together

  1. A network is layers of neurons; each neuron takes a weighted sum of its inputs and applies a non-linear activation function. The weights and biases are what it learns.
  2. A forward pass turns an input into a prediction; the loss function scores how wrong that prediction is.
  3. Backpropagation works out the slope of the loss for every weight; gradient descent nudges each weight downhill. Repeat over many epochs, and the loss falls: that is “training”.
  4. Regularization and a validation set stop the network from memorizing its training data; the right evaluation metric tells you whether it actually works for your purpose.

The thread back to Lecture 7A

One neuron with a sigmoid activation and cross-entropy loss is logistic regression. A neural network is many of them, stacked, and trained the same way.
